subject: Best 5-year fixed sits at 4.34% as yields climb
bodyMarkdown:
If you have a mortgage renewal coming up in the next year, the number that sets your payment moved again last week, and the Bank of Canada had nothing to do with it.

## Where your fixed rate actually comes from

A five-year fixed mortgage is funded with money the lender borrows for roughly five years, so it is priced off the five-year Government of Canada **bond yield** (the annual return a buyer earns for holding that government debt) rather than the overnight rate that makes the headlines. The Bank of Canada left the overnight rate at 2.25 per cent on September 2, its seventh hold in a row, and it has not moved the rate since October 2025. Fixed mortgage rates climbed anyway. Ratehub listed the best high-ratio five-year fixed in Canada (less than 20 per cent down, so it has to be insured) at 4.34 per cent as of Saturday, while nesto showed its lowest insured five-year fixed at 4.39 per cent on Thursday and put the Big Six bank average on the same term at 5.03 per cent. That spread of about 70 basis points is the piece a borrower can actually control.

## Oil is doing the pushing

The move in yields is coming from oil and from Washington. Brent crude has been trading above $100 a barrel through the Middle East conflict, and on Friday it eased a little over 1 per cent on reports that talks between Iran and American mediators might reach a conclusion. Even with that pullback, BOE Report wrote on Friday that bond yields were sitting at multi-decade highs. Canada's ten-year yield finished the day near 3.95 per cent, down about 4.7 basis points, after a week investors spent reassessing how expensive borrowing had suddenly become. The second push is the Fed, which raised its target range a quarter point to 3.75 to 4 per cent on September 16, its first increase since 2023. Canadian yields track American ones closely, so a Fed hiking into higher energy prices drags our mortgage market along with it.

## Housing was already flat

Canadian housing did not need higher fixed rates. CREA reported on September 15 that August home sales fell 6.9 per cent from a year earlier to 37,504, down 0.7 per cent from July, the fourth straight month in which sales and prices barely moved, with active listings just under 200,000. Toronto looks softer than the country as a whole. The city benchmark price was $918,400 in August, 3.7 per cent below a year earlier, and the average sale price was $979,684. Put those numbers beside a rising fixed rate and you get the standoff I see around Richmond Hill. Sellers watch prices drift down and refuse to cut. Buyers get quoted a higher rate every few weeks and decide to wait another season. Nobody is forced to move, so nothing moves.

## The takeaway

If you renew within the next year, get a rate hold now, since most lenders will guarantee a quoted rate for 90 to 120 days and you give up nothing if rates fall before you sign. Shop that 70 basis point gap instead of taking your own bank's first number, because 4.34 against 5.03 per cent on a $600,000 mortgage is a few hundred dollars every month. Watch Brent crude and the five-year Government of Canada yield rather than Bank of Canada meeting dates, because those two move first and the mortgage rate follows them. If the Iran talks go somewhere, fixed rates should ease within a few weeks, and if they fall apart, this gets worse before it gets better.
